justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon—one day (1d), one week (1w), and one month (1m)—were driven by what I anticipate to be the central or most likely outcomes based on available information and trends in the underlying dynamics of the variable being forecasted. For the short-term (1d), the point estimate reflects a relatively high degree of confidence in the near-term trajectory of the system, as short time horizons are often less exposed to sudden changes. Over one week (1w), the estimate incorporates a slightly broader range of potential deviations as the system has more time to drift away from its current state. By the one-month (1m) timeframe, the point estimate reflects a more aggregated and directional trend over time, while acknowledging broader long-term influences.

The confidence interval widths at each horizon, or the bounds of uncertainty (90% CI), generally widen as the forecast extends further into the future. This is because uncertainty tends to compound as more time passes, introducing more unknowns into the system. For instance, short-term uncertainties—like small fluctuations or noise—may have less time to accumulate over one day but become more impactful over a week. Over a month, macro-level variability, structural shifts, or cumulative noise become much more prominent drivers of uncertainty, which is why the one-month range is substantially wider. Additionally, any randomness inherent to the system or external shocks is harder to predict over longer periods.

Certain risks or events could cause outcomes to fall outside of these intervals, particularly in the longer-term forecast. These might include major and unanticipated events, such as policy changes, large market shocks, or external factors that directly influence the system in question (e.g., geopolitical events, natural disasters, or significant technological changes). Sometimes, the model itself may also be underestimating some types of uncertainty—like nonlinear responses or feedback loops—which could lead to unforeseen jumps or drops outside the predicted ranges. The farther out the forecast horizon, the more susceptible it is to these types of tail risks, which is why long-term scenarios require an even greater level of caution when interpreting the intervals.
